title: Adam, Nuh, Ibrahim and Yusuf
bigQuestion: How does the Qur'an tell the stories of the early prophets, and how are they like the Bible's stories?

story.title: Eleven Stars, the Sun and the Moon
story.kicker: A boy has a strange dream, and his father tells him to keep it secret.
paragraphs: A boy wakes up early. He runs to find his father. "Father," he says, "I saw eleven stars in my dream. I saw the sun and the moon too. They were all bowing down to me." His father listens carefully. He does not laugh. He looks worried and proud at the same time.

"My son," the father says, "do not tell your brothers about this dream. They might grow jealous. They might plan something against you." The boy has eleven brothers. His father loves him very much, and the brothers know it. The father thinks the dream means something big is coming.

The boy is Yusuf (Joseph). His father is Yaqub (Jacob). The Qur'an tells this story in Surah 12, a chapter named Yusuf. It calls the story "the best of stories." It is the only long story the Qur'an tells from beginning to end in one surah. Muslims read it in Ramadan and at home.

The Bible tells about Joseph too, in the book of Genesis. In the Bible, Joseph also dreams of eleven stars, the sun and the moon. Jews, Christians and Muslims all know this boy. But each book tells his story in its own way. In this chapter, you will read how the Qur'an tells about Adam, Nuh, Ibrahim and Yusuf.
story.think: Why do you think the father tells Yusuf to keep his dream a secret from his brothers?

lessons.title: What a Prophet Is
lessons.mainIdea: Muslims believe God sent many prophets to bring people the same message, and the Qur'an names 25 of them.
reading: A *prophet* is a person who brings a message from God. Muslims believe God sent prophets to every people. The Qur'an says that some prophets are named in the book and some are not. It names 25 prophets. Some are called messengers too, because Muslims believe they brought a book or a new law.

Many of the prophets in the Qur'an are people the Bible tells about. The Qur'an gives their names in Arabic. Adam is Adam. Nuh is Noah. Ibrahim is Abraham. Yusuf is Joseph. Musa is Moses. Isa is Jesus. Muslims believe the last prophet was Muhammad.

Muslims believe all the prophets taught one message. The message is that there is one God, and people should worship God and be good. In the Qur'an, God tells the prophets' stories to Muhammad. The Qur'an says the stories are lessons for people who think (12:111, Surah Yusuf).

words.d: a person who brings a message from God; Muslims believe there were many prophets
in Muslim belief, a prophet who brings a book or a new law from God
a chapter of the Qur'an; there are 114

look.title: Surahs Named for Prophets
look.cite: Chapter names and numbers in the standard Qur'an (Cairo edition, 1924)
look.prompt: Which of these surahs comes closest to the front of the book? Which comes near the end?

check.q: What is a prophet, in Muslim belief?
choices: A person who brings a message from God
A king who rules a city
An angel who lives in heaven
check.why: In the Qur'an, a prophet is a person chosen to bring God's message to people.

check.q: How many prophets does the Qur'an name?
check.why: The Qur'an names 25 prophets; 114 is the number of surahs.

check.q: Which name is the Arabic name for Abraham?
check.why: Ibrahim is Abraham; Nuh is Noah, Musa is Moses and Isa is Jesus.

lessons.title: Stories Shared by Three Books
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an, the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Bible tell about many of the same people, each in its own way.
reading: Jews read the *Hebrew Bible*. Christians read the Bible, which has the Old Testament and the New Testament. Muslims read the Qur'an. All three books tell about Adam, Noah, Abraham and Joseph. That is one reason people call Judaism, Christianity and Islam "Abrahamic" faiths.

The books do not tell the stories the same way. The Bible tells a story in order, from start to finish, with many details. The Qur'an usually tells a short part of a story. It often tells the same story in more than one surah. It says what the story teaches.

The Qur'an says that God sent earlier books too. Muslims believe God gave the *Torah* to Musa (Moses). They believe God gave the Gospel to Isa (Jesus). Muslims call Jews and Christians "People of the Book." In this chapter you will compare the tellings.

words.d: the holy book of Judaism; Christians call most of it the Old Testament
the first five books of the Hebrew Bible; Muslims believe God gave a Torah to Musa
the Qur'an's name for Jews and Christians, who have holy books too

look.title: Two Ways to Tell a Story
look.text: Imagine two friends tell you about the same soccer game. One tells you every play, from the first kick to the last whistle. The other says, "Our team was losing. Then we kept trying and won. Never give up." The Bible often tells a story the first way. The Qur'an often tells it the second way.
look.prompt: Which way of telling would you use to teach a lesson? Which way would you use to share the whole story?

check.q: Which three religions share stories about Adam, Noah and Abraham?
check.why: Judaism, Christianity and Islam all tell about these figures; that is why they are called Abrahamic faiths.

check.q: How does the Qur'an usually tell a story from the Bible?
choices: In short parts, often in more than one surah
In one long book from start to finish
As a poem with no lesson
check.why: The Qur'an usually tells a short part of a story and says what it teaches; the Bible tells more of the story in order.

check.q: Whom does the Qur'an call "People of the Book"?
check.why: The Qur'an uses "People of the Book" for Jews and Christians, who have holy books.

lessons.title: Adam, the First Person
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an says God made Adam, taught him the names of things, and told the angels to bow to him.
reading: The Qur'an says God made Adam, the first person, and made him a *khalifa* on the earth. That word means someone who takes care of something for someone else. God taught Adam the names of all things. Then God told the *angels* to bow to Adam. They bowed (2:30–34, Surah Al-Baqarah).

One being did not bow. His name was *Iblis*. The Qur'an says he was proud. He said he was made of fire and Adam was made of clay. Muslims believe Iblis became Shaytan, the one who whispers to people to do wrong (7:11–18, Surah Al-A'raf).

Adam and his wife lived in a garden. God told them not to eat from one tree. Iblis tricked them, and they ate. They said sorry to God. The Qur'an says God forgave them and sent them to live on the earth (2:35–37; 7:19–25). The Qur'an does not give Adam's wife a name. Muslim tradition calls her Hawwa (Eve).

words.d: a caretaker; the Qur'an says God made Adam a caretaker of the earth
beings Muslims believe God made from light to serve and carry messages
the being who, the Qur'an says, refused to bow to Adam out of pride

look.title: The Angels Bow
look.text: The Qur'an says that God told the angels He was going to put a caretaker on the earth. The angels asked why, since people would do harm. God said, "I know what you do not know." Then God taught Adam the names of all things and told the angels to bow to him.
look.cite: Qur'an 2:30–34, Surah Al-Baqarah (The Cow), told in simple words after Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: What does God teach Adam before the angels bow? Why might that matter in the story?

check.q: In the Qur'an, what did God teach Adam?
check.why: The Qur'an (2:31) says God taught Adam the names of all things; the boat belongs to Nuh's story.

check.q: Who refused to bow to Adam, according to the Qur'an?
check.why: The Qur'an says Iblis refused out of pride; Jibril is the angel who Muslims believe brought the Qur'an.

check.q: What does the Qur'an say happened after Adam and his wife ate from the tree?
choices: They said sorry and God forgave them
They sailed away in an ark
check.why: The Qur'an (2:37) says Adam turned to God and God forgave him; then they lived on the earth.

lessons.title: Adam in Two Books
lessons.mainIdea: The Bible and the Qur'an both tell about Adam and the garden, but they tell some parts differently.
reading: The Bible tells about Adam in the book of Genesis, chapters 2 and 3. There, a snake tells Eve to eat from the tree. Eve eats first and then gives some to Adam. God sends them out of the garden. Many Christians read this as the start of sin for all people.

The Qur'an tells the story in a shorter way. It says Shaytan whispered to both of them. It does not say the wife ate first. It says they both did wrong, both said sorry, and God forgave them. Most Muslim readers say each person is responsible for their own deeds, not for Adam's.

Both books agree on a lot. Both say God made Adam. Both tell about a garden and a tree. Both say the first people did wrong. When you *compare* two tellings, look for what is the same and what is different. Then ask what each book wants its readers to learn.

words.d: the first book of the Bible; it tells about Adam, Noah, Abraham and Joseph
to look at two things and find what is alike and what is different

look.title: Side by Side: The Garden
look.text: Genesis 3 says: a serpent speaks to the woman; she eats and gives to the man; God sends them out of the garden. The Qur'an (2:35–37; 7:20–23) says: Shaytan whispers to them both; they both eat; they both say they did wrong; God forgives them and sends them to live on the earth.
look.prompt: Name one thing the two tellings share and one thing that is different.

check.q: Where does the Bible tell the story of Adam?
check.why: Genesis, the first book of the Bible, tells about Adam; Surah Al-Baqarah is in the Qur'an.

check.q: In the Qur'an's telling, who is tricked into eating from the tree?
check.why: The Qur'an says Shaytan whispered to both, and both ate and both asked forgiveness.

check.q: What is one thing both the Bible and the Qur'an say about Adam?
choices: He was a king of Egypt
He lived in a garden with a tree he was told not to eat from
check.why: Both books tell about a garden and a forbidden tree; the ark is Noah's story and the eleven sons belong to Yusuf's father.

lessons.title: Nuh and the Ark
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an says Nuh warned his people for a long time, built an ark, and was saved from a flood with those who believed.
reading: The Qur'an tells about *Nuh* (Noah) in many surahs. One whole surah, Surah 71, is named Nuh. The Qur'an says Nuh told his people to worship one God. He warned them for a very long time. The Qur'an says he stayed among them 950 years (29:14, Surah Al-Ankabut). Most of them laughed at him.

God told Nuh to build an *ark*, a big boat. The Qur'an says people made fun of him while he built it. Then the flood came. Nuh took pairs of animals and the people who believed with him. The Qur'an says one of Nuh's sons would not get in. He said he would climb a mountain. The water covered him (11:36–43, Surah Hud).

The Qur'an says the ark came to rest on a mountain called Judi (11:44). The Bible tells about Noah in Genesis, chapters 6 to 9. In the Bible, the ark rests on the mountains of Ararat, and all of Noah's sons are saved. The Qur'an adds the son who would not believe. It uses the story to teach that each person must choose.

words.d: the prophet Noah; the Qur'an says he built an ark and was saved from a flood
a very large boat; in both the Bible and the Qur'an, Noah builds one
water that covers the land; both books tell about a great flood in Noah's time

look.title: The Son Who Would Not Board
look.text: The Qur'an says the ark sailed on waves like mountains. Nuh called to his son, who stood apart, "My son, come aboard with us." The son said he would climb a mountain to keep safe from the water. Nuh said that nothing could keep anyone safe that day but God's mercy. Then a wave came between them.
look.cite: Qur'an 11:42–43, Surah Hud, told in simple words after Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: What does the son think will save him? What does Nuh say will save people?

check.q: Which surah is named for Nuh?
check.why: Surah 71 is named Nuh; Surah 12 is Yusuf and Surah 19 is Maryam.

check.q: What does the Qur'an say Nuh did for a very long time before the flood?
choices: Warned his people to worship one God
check.why: The Qur'an says Nuh warned his people for many years; smashing idols is Ibrahim's story.

check.q: What is one difference between the Qur'an's Nuh story and the Bible's Noah story?
choices: The Qur'an tells of a son who would not board and was lost
The Bible says Noah was a prophet in Mecca
check.why: The Qur'an (11:42–43) tells about a son of Nuh who refused to board; Genesis says all of Noah's sons were saved.

lessons.title: Ibrahim and the Idols
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an says Ibrahim broke his people's idols to show they had no power, and God kept him safe from the fire.
reading: *Ibrahim* (Abraham) is one of the most important prophets in the Qur'an. His father's people prayed to *idols*. Idols are statues that people treat as gods. The Qur'an says Ibrahim asked them why. The idols could not hear, see or help them (21:52–67, Surah Al-Anbiya).

One day, the Qur'an says, Ibrahim broke all the idols but the biggest one. When people asked who did it, he said, "Ask the big one!" They knew the idol could not talk. Ibrahim wanted them to see that the idols had no power. The people got angry and threw him into a fire.

The Qur'an says God told the fire to be cool and safe for Ibrahim, and he was not hurt (21:69). The Bible does not tell this story. But old Jewish stories, called midrash, tell of Abraham breaking idols too. The Qur'an calls Ibrahim a *hanif*, a person who turned to the one God and away from idols.

words.d: the prophet Abraham; the Qur'an calls him a friend of God
a statue or object that people pray to as a god
the Qur'an's word for a person who turns to the one God and away from idols

look.title: Ask the Big One
look.text: The Qur'an says Ibrahim broke the idols into pieces, all but the biggest one. When the people asked who had done this, Ibrahim said the big one had done it, and told them to ask the idols if they could speak. The people looked at each other and knew that the idols could not speak.
look.cite: Qur'an 21:58–65, Surah Al-Anbiya (The Prophets), told in simple words after Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: What did Ibrahim want the people to notice about their idols?

check.q: What is an idol?
choices: A statue people pray to as a god
check.why: An idol is a statue or object treated as a god; the Qur'an says Ibrahim's people prayed to idols.

check.q: In the Qur'an, what happened when Ibrahim was thrown into the fire?
choices: The angels put it out with rain
God made the fire cool and safe for him
check.why: The Qur'an (21:69) says God told the fire to be cool and safe for Ibrahim.

check.q: Does the Bible tell the story of Abraham breaking the idols?
choices: No; it is in the Qur'an and in old Jewish stories, not in the Bible
Yes, in the Gospel of Luke
check.why: The idol story is in the Qur'an and in Jewish midrash; Genesis 22 tells about Abraham and his son on the mountain.

lessons.title: The Test With His Son
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an says Ibrahim dreamed he must give up his son, both agreed to obey God, and God gave a ram in the son's place.
reading: The Qur'an tells about a hard test. Ibrahim dreamed that he must give up his son as an offering to God. He told his son about the dream. The son said, "Father, do what you are told. You will find me patient" (37:102, Surah As-Saffat). They both agreed to obey God.

When Ibrahim laid his son down, God called to him. God said he had already done what the dream asked. The Qur'an says God gave a great animal to offer in the son's place (37:103–107). Muslims believe this shows how much Ibrahim trusted God.

The Qur'an does not say which son it was. Most Muslim scholars say it was *Ismail* (Ishmael), Ibrahim's older son. Some early Muslim scholars said it was Ishaq (Isaac). The Bible, in Genesis 22, names the son as Isaac. Jews and Christians read the story with Isaac. Muslims and Jews and Christians all see it as a story about trust in God.

words.d: the prophet Ishmael, Ibrahim's older son; most Muslims say he was the son in the test
the prophet Isaac, Ibrahim's younger son; the Bible names him as the son on the mountain
something given up to God

look.title: One Story, Two Names
look.text: Genesis 22 says God tells Abraham to take "your son, your only son Isaac" up a mountain. The Qur'an (37:100–111) tells the dream and the test but does not name the son. Right after the story, it says God gave Ibrahim good news of Ishaq. Many Muslim scholars read that to mean the son in the test was Ismail, born before Ishaq. Others have read it differently.
look.prompt: Why might the same story have a different son's name in two books? What does each book keep the same?

check.q: In the Qur'an, how did Ibrahim learn he was to give up his son?
choices: An angel came in the daytime
He read it in a book
check.why: The Qur'an (37:102) says Ibrahim saw it in a dream and told his son.

check.q: What did the son say when Ibrahim told him the dream?
choices: He ran away to the mountains
He said the dream was not true
He said his father should do what he was told, and he would be patient
He asked his brothers for help
check.why: The Qur'an says the son agreed to obey God and told his father he would be patient.

check.q: Which book names the son in the test as Isaac?
check.why: Genesis 22 names Isaac; the Qur'an does not name the son, and most Muslim scholars say Ismail.

lessons.title: Building the Kaaba, and Eid al-Adha
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an says Ibrahim and Ismail built the Kaaba, and Muslims remember Ibrahim's test each year at Eid al-Adha.
reading: The *Kaaba* is a square stone building in Mecca. Muslims face it when they pray. The Qur'an says Ibrahim and his son Ismail raised its walls and prayed that God would accept their work (2:127, Surah Al-Baqarah). Muslims believe it is the first house built for worshiping the one God.

Every year, Muslims from around the world go to Mecca for the *hajj*. It is a special trip. Many things they do there remember Ibrahim's family. They walk between two hills. Muslim tradition says Ismail's mother Hajar did that. She was looking for water for her baby.

At the end of the hajj comes *Eid al-Adha*, "the feast of the offering." Muslims everywhere celebrate it, not just in Mecca. Families who can afford it give an animal. They share the meat and give some to people in need. It remembers the day Ibrahim was ready to give up his son. In Chicago, families gather for morning prayers and visit each other.

words.d: the square stone building in Mecca that Muslims face when they pray
the trip to Mecca that Muslims try to make once in their lives
the feast of the offering; a holiday that remembers Ibrahim's test

look.title: A Holiday With a Story Inside
look.text: Picture a morning in a Chicago neighborhood. Families walk to a big hall in new clothes. After prayers, they hug and say "Eid Mubarak," which means "blessed feast." Later, meat is packed in bags. One bag goes to the family, one to friends, and one to people who need food. Every part of the day points back to a story about Ibrahim.
look.prompt: Which part of Eid al-Adha connects to the story of Ibrahim's test? Which part helps other people?

check.q: Who does the Qur'an say built the Kaaba?
check.why: The Qur'an (2:127) says Ibrahim and Ismail raised the walls of the House.

check.q: What does Eid al-Adha remember?
check.why: Eid al-Adha, the feast of the offering, remembers the day Ibrahim was ready to give up his son.

check.q: What do many families do with meat on Eid al-Adha?
choices: Keep all of it at home
Share it and give some to people in need
check.why: Families who give an animal share the meat with friends and with people who need food.

lessons.title: The Well and Egypt
lessons.mainIdea: Surah 12 tells how Yusuf's brothers put him in a well, and how he was carried to Egypt and wrongly put in prison.
reading: Surah 12 is the only surah that tells one story from start to finish. It has 111 ayahs. It begins by calling itself "the best of stories." Then it tells Yusuf's dream, the one you read at the start of this chapter. His father, Yaqub, warned him not to tell his brothers.

The brothers were *jealous*. They asked to take Yusuf out to play. Then they put him in a well. They came home crying and said a wolf ate him. They showed their father Yusuf's shirt with fake blood on it. Yaqub did not believe them. He said, "Patience is beautiful" (12:18).

A *caravan* stopped at the well for water and found Yusuf. They sold him in Egypt to a rich man. Later the man's wife tried to make Yusuf do wrong. Yusuf refused. The Qur'an says his shirt was torn from the back, which showed he was running away. Even so, he was put in prison. The Qur'an does not name the man or his wife. The Bible calls the man Potiphar.

words.d: wanting what someone else has; Yusuf's brothers were jealous of their father's love
a group of people and animals traveling together to trade
waiting calmly through hard times; Yaqub said "patience is beautiful"

look.title: The Best of Stories
look.text: At the start of Surah 12, the Qur'an says that God is telling Muhammad the best of stories by revealing this Qur'an to him. Then Yusuf tells his father he saw eleven stars, the sun and the moon bowing to him. His father tells him not to tell his brothers, or they may plot against him.
look.cite: Qur'an 12:3–5, Surah Yusuf (Joseph), told in simple words after Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: Who is telling the story to whom, according to the surah's opening?

check.q: What makes Surah 12 different from most surahs?
choices: It tells one whole story from start to finish
check.why: Surah Yusuf is the only surah that tells one long story in order.

check.q: What did the brothers show their father to make him think Yusuf was dead?
check.why: The Qur'an (12:18) says they brought his shirt with false blood on it.

check.q: How did Yusuf get to Egypt in the Qur'an's telling?
choices: He walked there with his father
A caravan found him in the well and sold him there
check.why: The Qur'an (12:19–20) says travelers found him in the well and sold him in Egypt.

lessons.title: Dreams, Prison and the King
lessons.mainIdea: In prison, Yusuf explained dreams, and the king's dream about cows brought him out to save Egypt from hunger.
reading: In prison, Yusuf met two men who had strange dreams. He told them what their dreams meant, and he told them about the one God. One man was set free, as Yusuf said. But that man forgot Yusuf for years, and Yusuf stayed in prison (12:36–42).

Then the king of Egypt had a dream. He saw seven fat cows eaten by seven thin cows, and seven green ears of grain and seven dry ones. Nobody could explain it. The freed man finally remembered Yusuf. Yusuf said there would be seven good years, then seven years of *famine*, when little food grows. He told them to store grain (12:43–49).

Yusuf asked that his name be cleared first. The wife who had lied said the truth: Yusuf had done nothing wrong (12:51). The king made Yusuf the one in charge of Egypt's storehouses. In the Bible, in Genesis 41, Pharaoh has the same dream and Joseph is also put in charge. The Qur'an says "the king"; the Bible says "Pharaoh."

words.d: a time when there is not enough food
a building where grain is kept for later

look.title: Yusuf's Story by the Numbers
rows: Fat cows in the king's dream
look.cite: Qur'an 12:4, 12:43–49 (Surah Yusuf); ayah count from the standard Cairo edition, 1924
look.prompt: Which of these numbers also appears in the Bible's telling of Joseph in Genesis 37 and 41?

check.q: What did Yusuf do for the two men in prison?
check.why: The Qur'an (12:36–41) says Yusuf explained the prisoners' dreams and told them about God.

check.q: What did the king's dream mean, according to Yusuf?
choices: The king would have seven sons
Seven good years, then seven years of famine
check.why: Yusuf said the seven fat and seven thin cows meant seven years of plenty and seven of famine.

check.q: What did Yusuf ask for before he came out of prison?
check.why: The Qur'an (12:50–51) says Yusuf wanted the truth known first; the wife then admitted he had done nothing wrong.

lessons.title: The Brothers Return
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an ends Yusuf's story with forgiveness: he tells his brothers there is no blame on them, and the family is together again.
reading: The famine reached Yusuf's family too. His brothers came to Egypt to buy grain. They did not know the man in charge was Yusuf. He knew them. He told them to bring their youngest brother, Binyamin (Benjamin), next time. When they did, Yusuf found a way to keep Binyamin with him (12:58–79).

At last Yusuf told them who he was. The brothers were afraid. Yusuf said, "There is no blame on you today. May God forgive you" (12:92). He sent his shirt home. When it touched his father's face, Yaqub, who had cried until he could not see, could see again (12:93–96).

The whole family came to Egypt. The Qur'an says Yusuf's parents and brothers bowed to him, and Yusuf said his childhood dream had come true (12:100). The Bible, in Genesis 45 to 47, also tells how Joseph forgave his brothers and brought the family to Egypt. Both books make *forgiveness* the end of the story.

words.d: Benjamin, Yusuf's youngest brother
letting go of anger at someone who did you wrong
when family or friends come together again after being apart

look.title: No Blame Today
look.text: When Yusuf's brothers learned who he was, they admitted they had done wrong. Yusuf answered that there would be no blame on them that day, and asked God to forgive them. He told them to take his shirt and lay it on their father's face, and their father would see again.
look.cite: Qur'an 12:91–93, Surah Yusuf (Joseph), told in simple words after Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: Yusuf had the power to punish his brothers. What did he choose instead, and why do you think the Qur'an ends the story this way?

check.q: What did Yusuf say to his brothers when they found out who he was?
choices: There is no blame on you today
He told them to leave Egypt
He asked for his shirt back
check.why: The Qur'an (12:92) has Yusuf forgive his brothers with the words that there is no blame on them that day.

check.q: What happened when Yusuf's shirt touched his father's face?
check.why: The Qur'an (12:96) says Yaqub's sight came back when the shirt was placed on his face.

check.q: How is the ending of the Qur'an's Yusuf story like the ending of the Bible's Joseph story?
choices: Joseph punishes his brothers in both
Joseph goes back to live in the well in both
The family stays apart in both
Joseph forgives his brothers and the family comes to Egypt in both
check.why: Both Surah 12 and Genesis 45–47 end with forgiveness and the family reunited in Egypt.

review.q: How many prophets does the Qur'an name?
review.why: The Qur'an names 25 prophets; 114 is the number of surahs.

review.q: Which surah tells one whole story from beginning to end?
review.why: Surah Yusuf tells Yusuf's story in order, in 111 ayahs.

review.q: According to the Qur'an, who refused to bow to Adam?
review.why: The Qur'an says Iblis refused out of pride.

review.q: What does the Qur'an say happened to the fire when Ibrahim was thrown in?
choices: God made it cool and safe
review.why: The Qur'an (21:69) says God told the fire to be cool and safe for Ibrahim.

review.q: Where does the Bible tell about Adam, Noah, Abraham and Joseph?
review.why: All four are in Genesis, the first book of the Bible.

review.q: What is one difference between the Qur'an and the Bible about Ibrahim's test?
choices: The Bible names the son as Isaac; the Qur'an does not name him
The Qur'an says the son ran away
review.why: Genesis 22 names Isaac; the Qur'an (37:100–111) does not name the son, and most Muslim scholars say Ismail.

review.q: Who does the Qur'an say built the Kaaba?
review.why: The Qur'an (2:127) says Ibrahim and Ismail raised its walls.

review.q: How does the Qur'an's Yusuf story end?
choices: Yusuf goes back to the well
Yusuf forgives his brothers and the family is together
review.why: Surah 12 ends with forgiveness (12:92) and the family reunited in Egypt.
